675.bp: Blockchains split data across multiple computers (shards) to handle more transactions, but moving accounts between shards causes the whole system to freeze temporarily. This paper solves that freeze problem so thousands of financial transactions can keep flowing even while accounts are being physically relocated—like rerouting airport connections while passengers keep arriving.
675.wh: When an account moves from one shard to another, the system must pause to ensure no one double-spends money or corrupts data. The more accounts you move at once, the bigger and longer the shutdown. But if you move them one at a time, you waste months of traffic slowdowns as transactions keep crossing between shards that the account already left.
675.ap: BIND works by keeping two separate queues of pending transactions—one for accounts currently moving, one for accounts already settled. This lets the system process settled transactions immediately while migrations happen in the background. It groups accounts into small batches based on how tightly they interact (which accounts send money to which), so each batch move fixes more cross-shard traffic at once without causing a long freeze.
675.ww: The key insight is that you don't need the whole system locked—only the specific part handling those moving accounts needs pausing. By isolating the migrants into their own queue, non-migrating accounts see zero disruption, and by batching accounts that talk to each other a lot, you solve more of the traffic problem per freeze.
675.po: In real Ethereum tests, this buys a 12% overall speed boost, cuts migration time to one-quarter its normal length, and reduces future cross-shard traffic by nearly a quarter. Blockchains can now shuffle accounts around during peak use without anyone noticing.

676.bp: When you send video, audio, and text over the internet together, bandwidth is precious. Instead of sending raw pixels and sound waves, what if you could distill each modality down to only the semantic meaning (what it's actually saying) that matters for the task at hand, and throw away the rest? That's the real-world goal: efficient, robust transmission of *meaning* rather than raw data.
676.wh: Video, audio, and text naturally carry different kinds of signal and noise. A naive approach sends everything, hoping the receiver reconstructs from it all. But under bad wireless conditions (noisy channels), when one modality drops out (no audio), or when the audio/video are slightly out of sync, that approach fails because it depends on all three modalities being perfect. You also don't know which details matter for your specific task.
676.ap: Grasp works by first segmenting the streams into meaningful blocks, then building a graph of how those blocks connect. A neural graph network then identifies three layers of information within each block: strongly relevant stuff (keep this), weakly relevant stuff (can discard), and noise (throw out). The system synchronizes video, audio, and text by comparing how similar they are across the three sources. At the receiver, if audio drops, the system reconstructs it from the shared meaning it stored, using what the video and text already told it.
676.ww: By disentangling signal into three tiers (task-relevant, background, noise), you're only sending the essential semantic core. This works because the three modalities overlap in meaning—if video says
the text knows what to expect, so it can reconstruct the audio's meaning even if the audio stream is corrupted. This graceful degradation is much more robust than sending everything.
676.po: The result is transmission that survives low signal-to-noise conditions where the original would fail, handles missing modalities (one stream drops, others compensate), and stays synchronized despite streaming asynchrony. Cross-modal tasks like video-based question answering work even on noisy wireless links.

677.bp: Phishing attacks cost billions per year—criminals impersonate banks and email services to steal passwords and credit card numbers. Understanding where attackers get their tools and share their techniques reveals what countermeasures will actually work. This paper does detective work on the dark web itself, reading the attackers' own forums to understand the supply chain *before* attacks happen.
677.wh: Most research studies phishing after the fact: 'here's a fake email we found, let's reverse-engineer it.' But that tells you nothing about how attackers learned to make it, where they bought the tools, which services are most targeted, or when new attack methods are spreading. The dark web forums are where attackers trade phishing kits (automated tools to set up fake login pages), buy stolen credentials, and share code snippets—but reading 394,000 posts by hand is impossible.
677.ap: The researchers collected 13 years of posts (2013–2025) from 13 dark web forums and used a language model to automatically extract the key information: 'this post mentions PayPal phishing,' 'this one sells an SMTP server for sending fake emails,' 'this author made a phishing kit.' They mapped everything onto a seven-stage attack playbook (acquire tools, build fake page, send emails, steal credentials, etc.) so they could see which components are easiest to find and which services are most under fire.
677.ww: By reading the supply chain backwards, you see what's actually bottlenecked. If stolen Gmail credentials are expensive and rare, that's one defense angle. If phishing-kit source code is freely shared, that's another. If PayPal is targeted 10x more than Netflix, defensive resources should follow the attacker's priorities. The dark web forums literally tell you the attacker's perspective, not the defender's guess.
677.po: The study maps 12 years of attack trends, revealing which services face the most pressure, how often attack components change, and where the attacker's supply chain has weak links. This data lets defenders predict which services will be hit next and which attack tools are about to become prevalent.

678.bp: Traffic prediction (how many cars will be on Fifth Avenue tomorrow at 3pm) powers navigation apps, traffic lights, and delivery logistics. But building a good traffic model is hard: you need one model for highways, another for city grids, another for rural roads. What if you could describe 'I need to predict city traffic' in English and have a system automatically design and build the right neural network for you?
678.wh: Traffic datasets vary wildly: different city layouts, different time patterns (rush hour vs. weekend), different prediction horizons (1 hour ahead vs. 1 week). Manually designing a neural network for each dataset takes months of tweaking. Even worse, a network that works for New York often fails for Beijing because the underlying patterns are different. You need modularity and reusability, but each problem feels bespoke.
678.ap: ST-LEGO is a system where multiple AI agents collaborate: one agent (Prompt Agent) reads your task description in natural language ('predict traffic on a grid'), another agent (Assemble Agent) picks modular components from a library (a module for time patterns, a module for spatial relationships, a module for special events), and a third agent (Code Agent) automatically writes PyTorch code that sticks these pieces together. The framework uses a standardized language to describe model architectures so pieces snap together reliably.
678.ww: The insight is that most traffic models are built from the same fundamental building blocks (time dynamics, spatial propagation, feature fusion). By separating the block descriptions from the plumbing code, you can ask a language model to design the assembly, not the wiring. The system learns which blocks work for which datasets automatically, rather than requiring a human expert.
678.po: Models built this way learn faster, achieve higher accuracy on multiple real traffic datasets, and can transfer to new cities with minimal retraining. The same system can generate diverse model architectures for different cities, beating hand-crafted baselines in both accuracy and convergence speed.

679.bp: Pre-trained neural network models are expensive to build (weeks of computing). When you get a new task (classify a different graph dataset), you want to reuse a pre-trained model rather than training from scratch. The question: without actually fine-tuning the model, can you quickly score whether it will work well on your new task, so you pick the best one from a shelf of candidates?
679.wh: For images and text, there are good ways to score model transferability quickly. But graphs are stranger: a graph's structure (who is connected to whom) is just as important as the features. When the new graph dataset has a different structure than the data the model was trained on (distribution shift), the pre-trained model's abilities break down in unpredictable ways. Existing scoring methods don't account for graph structure at all.
679.ap: GNNMTE scores a model's transferability by decomposing the pre-trained model's learned structure using mathematical techniques (singular value decomposition) to extract its core learned patterns. It then weights these patterns based on their importance for the new graph dataset, and measures how well these patterns align with the new graph's own structure. The score tells you whether the model learned universals that will transfer, or task-specific quirks that won't.
679.ww: The core idea is that good models learn abstract structural principles (like 'nodes with many connections matter more'). By decomposing what the model learned and comparing it to your new graph's structure, you're checking whether the model's learned abstractions match your new graph's reality. If they do, transfer will work.
679.po: You can now score multiple pre-trained GNN models in seconds and pick the one most likely to transfer well, without waiting weeks for fine-tuning experiments. This is especially valuable when you only have small graph datasets where training from scratch is infeasible.

680.bp: Graph neural networks learn node representations by comparing nodes to their neighbors. But this approach struggles to capture complex, multi-hop patterns—like 'nodes that form triangles are different from nodes in chains even if they have the same direct neighbors.' This paper teaches networks to reason about these higher-order structures so they build richer, more informative node descriptions.
680.wh: A node's immediate neighbors are obvious, but what about neighbors-of-neighbors? Standard graph learning ignores these distant patterns, losing critical structural information. When you try to add them, you run into three problems: (1) you need to explicitly preserve edges that define higher-order structures but might seem unimportant locally, (2) you can't tell which nodes matter for which structures, and (3) when you artificially create negative examples to train on, they're indistinguishable from real ones.
680.ap: SPGCL identifies small graph patterns (subgraph patterns like triangles, chains, stars) that encode high-order structure. It keeps edges that are crucial for these patterns, even if they seem low-value locally. It then encodes each node, edge, and connection matrix with information about which patterns they participate in. During training, it treats nodes that are in different pattern families as dissimilar and nodes in the same patterns as similar, making negative examples actually discriminative.
680.ww: The insight is that high-order structures have geometric meaning: a triangle node and a chain node behave fundamentally differently even with identical neighborhoods. By explicitly tagging nodes with their role in common patterns and forcing the model to discriminate between different pattern families, you're forcing it to learn structure, not just density.
680.po: Nodes now have richer representations that capture both local neighborhoods and global structural roles. On six real-world datasets, this beats all existing methods and learns representations that better separate nodes with different roles.

681.bp: Recommending micro-videos (TikTok, Instagram Reels) means handling video (visual), audio, and text together. The challenge: videos have messy, noisy interactions (users might click out of boredom, not dislike), and the multimodal features often overlap confusingly—visual and audio might both encode 'music genre,' which is redundant. You want to clean up both the noise and the redundancy to make recommendations more accurate.
681.wh: Existing systems assume the user-video interactions are clean and all three modalities (visual, audio, text) tell independent stories. In reality, many clicks are noise (misclicks, scrolling too fast), and the modalities share information (a song's title and the audio beat both tell you it's pop music). This redundancy means the model wastes effort learning the same thing three times, and noise in the interaction graph corrupts the signal about what users actually want.
681.ap: MBGSL learns the 'true' interaction graph by denoising the raw data—instead of treating clicks as gospel, it learns which interactions are actually meaningful. For each modality (visual, audio, text), it learns a separate view of the graph, each optimized to remove redundant information within that modality. Then it compares across modalities to identify and remove the shared signal that appears in multiple views. The model simultaneously learns representations and graph structure, using shared semantic principles across modalities to guide both.
681.ww: By learning the graph structure instead of trusting raw clicks, you're doing supervised denoising—keeping interactions that make sense given the video content, discarding noise. By removing intra-modality redundancy and inter-modality overlap, you force each modality to contribute unique information, so all three together paint a complete picture without waste.
681.po: Videos get richer, cleaner representations. Recommendations improve on three real datasets by beating existing methods, especially in identifying which videos users truly like versus accidentally clicked.

682.bp: Imagine you observe a cascade of rumors spreading through Twitter, but you didn't see how the rumors moved (no direct friendship graph). Can you reconstruct the hidden network by just watching which accounts got infected in what order? The real-world use: inferring social network structure, disease spread networks, or influence patterns from the outcomes alone.
682.wh: If you have just one cascade (1000 tweets about one rumor), there's not enough information to uniquely determine the network—many possible networks could produce the same spread pattern. But here's the key insight: in the real world, multiple cascades happen on the *same underlying network*. Most methods give up and infer each cascade's network independently, wasting the mutual information. When you have little data per cascade, this independence assumption hurts badly.
682.ap: The paper proposes an iterative algorithm: start by inferring each cascade independently (standard approach). Then, use the fact that cascades share a network to update all inferences together—if cascade 1 suggests 'A talks to B,' and cascade 2 confirms it, boost that link's confidence. Repeat this refinement until the inferences stabilize. The algorithm guarantees that each iteration improves, so you know it converges to a stable solution.
682.ww: The insight is that multiple weak signals reinforce each other. One cascade might not uniquely specify a link, but the same link appearing in 10 cascades as the best explanation is strong evidence. By jointly optimizing all inferences, you're using global consistency as a regularizer—individual cascades stay consistent with each other because they all come from the same network.
682.po: You can now reconstruct networks from limited cascade data (few observations per cascade) with higher accuracy than single-cascade methods. This is valuable when you have many small cascades (many conversations, few replies each) rather than a few mega-viral events.

683.bp: Web agents are AI systems that use tools (click buttons, type text, run code) in long sequences to complete real tasks—booking flights, debugging code, researching topics. These agents need to learn to explore different tool options when uncertain, but be decisive when confident. The challenge: balancing exploration and decisiveness so training doesn't collapse into nonsense.
683.wh: A naive training approach says: 'when the model is uncertain, try different tools (explore).' But this leads to thrashing: the agent spends 50 steps trying every tool instead of committing to one. The model also learns to be uncertain as a hedging strategy, which sounds safe but actually prevents learning. Existing algorithms can't handle this 'exploration-greediness tradeoff' on long, multi-step tasks.
683.ap: AEPO (Agentic Entropy-Balanced Policy Optimization) has two parts. First, during exploration (generating training examples), it monitors the model's uncertainty and actively limits over-exploration: if the model is uncertain about consecutive steps, it penalizes that to prevent thrashing. Second, during learning from those examples, it carefully handles high-uncertainty steps by preserving learning signal on uncertain decisions while preventing runaway gradient updates that would destabilize training.
683.ww: The key is treating uncertainty strategically: it's good for exploring diverse solutions, bad for committing to sequences. By pre-monitoring uncertainty and imposing a 'no thrashing' penalty, you force the model to commit some of the time. By separately scaling learning on uncertain steps, you let the model learn *why* it should be uncertain in some cases while preventing that learned uncertainty from metastasizing.
683.po: On 14 real web tasks, this beats seven other RL algorithms by maintaining stable training and learning diverse solutions while avoiding collapse. The agent learns when to explore and when to commit, producing more reliable long-horizon behavior.

684.bp: Recommendation systems today optimize for clicks and time spent—'show them content they'll engage with.' But engagement doesn't mean the user trusts the system or feels in control. This paper builds a framework to ask the harder question: does this recommender respect the user as a person, or does it just manipulate engagement?
684.wh: Metrics like 'clicks' and 'dwell time' perversely reward making users addicted, showing them outrage even if it harms them, or manipulating them into clicking things they'll regret. These metrics also don't care about transparency (does the user understand why they were shown this?) or agency (could the user have gotten a different view if they wanted?). You can optimize engagement and leave users feeling trapped and mistrustful.
684.ap: The paper develops a human-centered evaluation framework that measures trust, agency, transparency, and satisfaction alongside engagement. They then qualitatively study an LLM-based recommender system, examining trade-offs: 'if we rank by diversity instead of just click-likelihood, engagement drops but users feel more respected. If we explain our recommendations, that takes screen space but users trust us more.' They explore how design choices (ranking strategy, diversity, transparency) affect these human-centered outcomes.
684.ww: The mechanism is simply asking the right questions: 'Did users feel respected by this system?' rather than just 'Did they click?' The framework makes visible what's been hidden—that you can't maximize engagement and trust simultaneously without careful design. By measuring both, you force designers to acknowledge the tradeoff.
684.po: The work surfaces concrete design choices (ranking, diversity, transparency mechanisms) that improve trust and satisfaction at the cost of some engagement. This gives recommender-system designers a vocabulary to reason about human impact, not just metrics.

685.bp: Training large language models is extremely expensive (millions of dollars in computing). What if multiple organizations (companies, universities, governments) pooled resources to train one model together, splitting costs and keeping their own data private? The challenge: how do you ensure each participant contributes fairly and gets rewarded justly without a central authority keeping score?
685.wh: In centralized training, one company controls everything and decides who did what. In decentralized federated training, no single authority can be trusted. How do you verify that participant A actually trained the model for 100 hours with quality data, while participant B only contributed 10 hours of junk data? How do you fairly split the final model's value? Without a trusted referee, participants can fake contributions or freeload.
685.ap: The system uses two mechanisms: (1) a mathematical formula (Shapley value) that fairly credits each participant's contribution by measuring how much the final model improves because of their data, and (2) blockchain smart contracts that automatically check contributions and pay rewards in tokens. Participants submit their data and compute hours, the system trains collaboratively, and then the smart contracts verify contributions and automatically pay each participant their earned tokens proportional to their impact.
685.ww: Shapley values work because they measure counterfactual contribution: 'if we trained without participant A, how much worse would the model be?' This credit is fair in a game-theoretic sense—no participant can gain by falsely reporting or withholding effort. Blockchain adds transparency: the payment logic is publicly verifiable code, not a black box.
685.po: Organizations can now collaborate on expensive AI training with automatic, transparent credit assignment and payment. Simulation results show more stable participation, fairer value distribution, and reduced financial concentration compared to centralized models.

686.bp: Machine learning services (MLaaS) let organizations use AI without building it themselves—pick a service, pay per query. But how do you choose between 10,000 services? And how do you combine them (use service A for preprocessing, B for predictions, C for confidence estimates)? This paper builds a data generator so researchers can test selection and combination algorithms at scale.
686.wh: Real MLaaS services vary wildly in cost, accuracy, latency, and specialty. You might pick the cheapest option and regret it when it times out, or pick the most accurate and go broke. Combining services is harder: which should run first? Do you need all three or can two suffice? Testing this requires spinning up thousands of real services, which is expensive and slow.
686.ap: MDG (MLaaS Dataset Generator) simulates realistic MLaaS behavior by training diverse machine-learning models across multiple real datasets. It records not just accuracy but costs, latencies, service composition patterns (how well service A's output feeds into B), and how services behave under different data conditions (drift, corrupted inputs). It then generates a dataset of 10,000+ synthetic service descriptions and results.
686.ww: By generating synthetic data that mimics the distributions of real MLaaS systems, you get a cheap, reproducible way to test selection and composition algorithms. The key is recording realistic quality-of-service metrics (latency, cost, availability), not just raw accuracy. This lets algorithms optimize for real tradeoffs—speed vs. accuracy, cost vs. reliability.
686.po: Researchers can now test MLaaS selection and composition algorithms on 10,000+ services without expensive real-world testing. The framework extends to IoT environments where services have unique constraints (low bandwidth, intermittent connectivity).

687.bp: Wireless sensor networks (thousands of temperature sensors across a city, or humidity sensors in a farm) often have missing data—sensors break, run out of battery, or turn off to save power. This creates gaps in the spatial-temporal readings you need for decision-making. How do you recover missing data while keeping individual sensor data private so no central authority sees raw measurements?
687.wh: Existing methods work well for recovery but require sending all sensor data to a central server, which raises privacy concerns—the cloud service sees everyone's exact measurements. Federated learning (each sensor trains locally and uploads only gradients) preserves privacy, but existing federated methods don't exploit the spatial-temporal structure of sensor networks, so recovery quality suffers.
687.ap: FLFL (Federated Latent Factor Learning) combines two ideas: each sensor locally learns latent factors (like 'temperature varies with time of day'), uploads only the gradient updates (not raw data), and the central server combines these gradients. Crucially, the model explicitly incorporates spatial-temporal correlation—neighboring sensors at similar times should have similar values—as a constraint during learning. This gives the model structure to exploit for better recovery without demanding raw data.
687.ww: The insight is that you can bake domain knowledge (spatial-temporal correlation) into the federated learning algorithm as a regularization constraint. This guides recovery without requiring raw data. Each sensor's privacy is protected because only gradients leave the device, but the model is much stronger because it reasons about how sensors relate across space and time.
687.po: Missing sensor values are recovered accurately (even when 30% of data is missing) while each sensor's raw measurements stay private—only gradient updates leave the device. This works for smart city applications, precision agriculture, and industrial monitoring.

688.bp: Online stories (serialized fiction, news articles) need advertisements inserted somewhere. But ads during climactic moments ruin the experience. What if you could detect whether a paragraph has high narrative tension (big reveal, emotional moment) so you avoid spoiling it with ads? This paper uses language models to identify tense moments automatically.
688.wh: Placing ads at random loses revenue (put an ad during a cliffhanger and readers abandon the story, so fewer ads are served). Placing ads only at story breaks loses opportunity (not every natural pause is good). Manually labeling every paragraph is infeasible for thousands of stories. You need an automatic way to score 'how tense is this paragraph?' so ad systems can avoid hot moments and place ads during calm transitions.
688.ap: The authors use a language model as a classifier trained on paragraphs labeled with narrative tension levels. The model learns to recognize cues like conflict escalation, revelation, character reactions, and time pressure. It scores each paragraph's tension so ad systems can insert breaks during low-tension passages and preserve high-tension sequences uninterrupted.
688.ww: Language models are good at recognizing narrative patterns because they've read billions of stories. By encoding narrative tension as a classification task, you're leveraging that prior knowledge. Identifying calm moments is easier than trying to manually craft rules—the model learns patterns humans would miss.
688.po: Ad placement systems can now avoid disrupting key story moments, preserving reader engagement while still serving ads during transitions. This keeps subscription revenue up and readers satisfied.

689.bp: Major social events (protests, epidemics, financial crashes) are rare but consequential. Early warning systems could mobilize resources before disaster, but events are so infrequent that building accurate predictions is nearly impossible—you have almost no positive examples to learn from. This paper uses intermediate signals (smaller, earlier events) to predict rare events before they happen.
689.wh: Standard machine learning assumes balanced classes, but rare events are the opposite: 1 in 100,000 events is a major crisis. Training with 99,999 non-events and 1 crisis, any model that says 'no crisis' is 99.99% accurate but useless. Even worse, you miss dependencies: a crisis isn't random—earlier, smaller tremors usually precede it. Most rare-event methods ignore these dependencies, treating each observation in isolation.
689.ap: Mediator Learning (ML) uses intermediate events as 'mediators'—like recognizing that before a major protest, you typically see smaller grievance-related posts. The system first extracts these mediator events using information theory (finding events that contain the most information about whether rare events follow), then builds a graph where smaller events flow up through mediators to rare events. A neural graph network models these tiers, where upper-level predictions (will a crisis happen?) are informed by lower-level probability distributions (how likely are the precursor tremors?).
689.ww: By explicitly routing through intermediate events, you're learning the causal chain rather than trying to predict rare events from nothing. A precursor is common (small protests are frequent), so it's easy to learn. The rare event becomes: 'if precursors reach a threshold, then crisis,' which is learnable. Mediators decompose the imbalanced problem into stages.
689.po: Rare-event prediction accuracy improves substantially by learning precursor-to-crisis chains. This matters for crisis detection: you can now predict rare social events like major unrest, epidemics, or financial shocks by watching for the preceding cascade of smaller signals.
